extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and companies evaluating or litigating software/computer-implemented patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether computer-implemented or software-related patent claims meet US §101 patent-eligibility after the Supreme Court's Alice decision by applying the Mayo two-step framework and related precedents (Bilski, Mayo, Flook, Myriad). Useful for claim drafting, prosecution risk assessment, and pre-suit scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Statute of the US defines patentable subject matter as ‘any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' and any improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory baseline is the starting point for eligibility analysis, but it is subject to judicially-created exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). The article cites 35 U.S.C. §101 as the statutory foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent cannot be granted for laws of nature, natural phenomena or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to these categories are treated as patent-ineligible regardless of fitting the statutory categories; court must analyze whether a claim is directed to such an exception before proceeding to further steps (see Mayo/Flook/Myriad/Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software patents: requirement of hardware/system element in many jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In most of the countries, software cannot be patented unless it forms an element within a hardware or a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: pure-software claims that do not tie the software to a particular machine or system are at higher risk of ineligibility. The article notes national differences and that Alice significantly curtailed software patentability in the US.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice holding: implementing an abstract idea on a computer does not make it patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court opined in Alice that an abstract idea could not be patented just because it is implemented on a computer; the software implementation of an escrow arrangement was not eligible because it is merely an implementation of an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims, courts will scrutinize whether the computer implementation is only an insignificant or conventional automation of an abstract practice; such implementations typically fail §101 after Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework — Step 1: determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first Mayo step, the court must determine if the patent claim at hand contains an abstract idea. If not, the claim is potentially patentable subject to other requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a threshold inquiry; if the claim is not directed to an abstract idea, no further Mayo-step-2 inventive-concept analysis is required for §101 eligibility (though other patentability requirements still apply). The article emphasizes correctly identifying ‘directed to’ versus merely involving an idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework — Step 2: determine whether the claim embodies an 'inventive concept'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second step analysis, the Court must determine whether the patent embodies the inventive concept — i.e., the implementation of the idea must not be generic, conventional or obvious and must add something that transforms the idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for elements or combinations that integrate the building blocks into something more; trivial token implementation (e.g., conventional computer hardware) will not qualify. The inventive concept must be sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation fails to transform an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: "Merely requiring generic computer implementation fails to transform [an] abstract idea into a patent eligible invention; mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform a patent-ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply recite using a generic computer to perform well-known steps should be treated as ineligible. Drafting should avoid claiming only standard computer components or generic automation as the novel feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Apply it' language is insufficient to confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating an abstract idea by adding the words 'apply it' is not enough for patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply phrasing a claim as 'apply the idea using a computer' or similar boilerplate will not meet §101 requirements after Alice; claims must show a non-generic, inventive implementation rather than mere application language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or trivial expedients do not support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The central and unique feature of the legal analysis of the Myriad and the Mayo case was that conventional or trivial expedients do not hold any weight in the patent-eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating inventive concept, courts will discount steps or elements that are well-understood, routine, or conventional; these cannot be relied on to render an otherwise abstract idea patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level/generalized claiming of routine features will not establish an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a well understood, routine and conventional feature at a higher level of generality does not suffice for an 'inventive concept'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters should avoid broad functional claiming that abstracts routine practice to a high level; instead, emphasize specific technical improvements, non-conventional architecture, or particular machine-oriented implementations that demonstrate a concrete inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation: scrutinize pre-Alice software patents before asserting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before filing a lawsuit for infringement of a software patent it is pertinent to scrutinize the claims in the light of the Alice case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many patents issued pre-Alice may be vulnerable under the Alice/Mayo framework, defendants-in-suit or patentees bringing suits should analyze whether claims are directed to abstract ideas and whether they include sufficient inventive concept; consider re-drafting, reexamination, or other risk mitigation steps.
